title: Day 1 · Start here + Tell me about yourself
lines: Hey Steven. Welcome to day one. Twelve days until Emory, and this is the track that starts it all.

Quick setup, and then we get to work. I'm your coach. I'll explain things, give you frameworks, and point out what's strong in your application. My partner here is your proctor. When he talks, he's the interviewer, and it's your turn to answer out loud.
That's me. I'll ask, you'll hear a chime, and that's your cue. Talk until you hear the second chime.
Out loud matters. Saying it in your head feels finished when it isn't. Mumbling in the car counts. Walking the dog counts. Just say it.

Today is the most common opener in every health professions interview: tell me about yourself. At Emory, it might come in a breakout with two or three faculty, or someone might ask it casually during the tour. Either way, it sets the tone for everything after it.

Here's the trap. Most people either recite their resume in order, or they tell their whole life story starting in grade school. Neither one works. What works is a short arc with a point. The interviewer should finish your answer knowing who you are right now, the one thread that ties your experiences together, and why that thread leads to this program.
So we're not writing a script. We're building beats. Four of them, in order. If you know the beats, you can say it a dozen different ways and it never sounds memorized.

Beat one. Who you are right now. One or two sentences. You're finishing exercise science at B Y U. You work as a scribe and medical assistant for a behavioral health startup in Orem. And you volunteer as a Spanish medical interpreter at a community clinic in Midvale. That's it. Present tense. No dates.

Beat two. The moment. This is your hook, and you already have a great one. The heart transplant you observed. You held a still-warm human heart, and then you spent the rest of the case at the head of the bed, and you realized there were two jobs happening at once. The surgeons replacing the heart, and anesthesia keeping the patient alive while they did it. Keep this to two or three sentences. Don't describe gore. Describe the realization.

Beat three. The thread. This is what makes your answer different from the other seven people in your session. Your thread is responsibility for people who can't care for themselves or speak for themselves. Caring for a quadriplegic client whose whole morning routine was a safety sequence. Interpreting, where you are literally someone's voice. Behavioral health and detox, where patients often can't advocate for themselves. Name the thread out loud, and give two quick examples. Not all of them.

Beat four. Why this, why now. You found the C A A role, you shadowed in Utah, and you watched a C A A carry that responsibility completely, with an anesthesiologist backing her up. The anesthetized patient is the extreme version of the thread. That's where you want to be. End there. Don't trail off. A clean ending sounds confident.
Total length, about a minute and a half. Under two, always.
Here's what a sample might sound like. Listen to the shape, not the exact words.

"I'm Steven. I'm finishing my exercise science degree at B Y U, and right now I work as a scribe and medical assistant for a behavioral health startup in Orem, and I volunteer as a Spanish interpreter at a community clinic in Midvale. I picked up my Spanish on a two-year mission in Ecuador."

"Medicine really got its hooks in me when I got to observe a heart transplant. I ended up at the head of the bed for most of it, and what stuck with me was that there were two jobs happening at once. The surgeons were replacing the heart, and anesthesia was keeping the patient alive while they did it."

"Looking back, most of what I've done since has been some version of taking responsibility for people who can't fully take care of themselves. I was a caregiver for a quadriplegic client. I interpret for patients who can't communicate with their doctor. I work with detox patients who aren't always in a place to speak for themselves."
"When I found the C A A role and started shadowing, it clicked. An anesthetized patient is the most complete version of that. So that's what brought me here."
Notice what that did. Present, moment, thread, destination. No G P A. No list of activities. They have your application. This is the story that makes the application make sense.
Your turn. First pass. Don't worry about being perfect. Just hit the four beats.
So, to get us started. Tell me a little about yourself.

How'd that feel? Quick check. Did you start with who you are now, not with your childhood? Did you name the thread out loud, in actual words, like responsibility for people who can't care for themselves? And did you stop cleanly, or did you trail off with something like, "so yeah, that's kind of me"? If you trailed off, that's the most common fix. Land on the destination and stop talking.
Now, the same question comes in disguises. Interviewers like to rephrase it, partly on purpose, to see if you're reciting. Same beats, different door. Here's one.
Walk me through how you got to this point. How did you end up applying to anesthesiologist assistant programs?

For that version, you can lean harder on beat four. They're asking about the path, so give a little more on how you discovered the role. Your brother-in-law is an anesthesiologist, so the care team idea was in your life before you ever pursued it. Then you shadowed, and you saw it firsthand. Keep the thread. Just let the path take more of the time.
One more disguise, and this one trips people up.
Tell me something about yourself that isn't in your application.

Good options for you here. You're married, and you and your wife are excited about a move east. You teach a youth Sunday school class, and you run it with questions instead of lectures. You play music. Any of those works. The goal is to show you're a real person who would be good to sit next to in class for twenty-seven months. Keep it to thirty seconds, and if you can, tie it back lightly. For example, teaching teenagers with questions has made you better at explaining things simply, which is exactly what you'll do with nervous patients.

Last drill for today. The thirty-second version. Sometimes a student or a faculty member asks it in the hallway or over refreshments, and two minutes would be too much. Compress it. One sentence per beat.
Hey, nice to meet you. So what's your story?

That's day one. Here's your homework, and it's light. Say the four beats out loud one more time today, maybe while you're driving. Present. Moment. Thread. Destination. Tomorrow is a listening day. You'll hear the history of the C A A profession and how the care team model actually works, so you can talk about it like an insider. See you then.

title: Day 2 · The CAA profession, past to present
lines: Day two. This one's a listening day. No pressure, just background you'll want in your pocket when an interviewer asks what you know about the profession. There's one quick practice question at the very end.
Let's start with where this whole thing came from.

In the mid nineteen sixties, the United States had a real shortage of anesthesia providers. Three anesthesiologists, all academic department chairs, looked at that problem and did something pretty clever. Their names were Joachim Gravenstein, John Steinhaus, and Perry Volpitto. Instead of just saying "we need more anesthesiologists," they broke anesthesia care down into its pieces. What tasks does this job involve, what education does each one need, and what level of responsibility does each one carry. From that analysis came the idea of a highly trained provider who would come from a pre-medical background and work under the direction of an anesthesiologist, as part of a team.

The first two programs opened in nineteen sixty-nine. One at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, and one at Emory, in Atlanta. Steinhaus was at Emory. So when you walk into Emory's building, you're walking into one of the two places where this profession started. Their website says "leading the way for fifty years," and that's not marketing fluff. It's literally true.

That's worth remembering, and it's worth mentioning if it fits naturally. Something like, "It means something to me to train at one of the programs that started the profession." Don't overdo it. One sentence.

Fast forward. In nineteen eighty-nine the National Commission for Certification of Anesthesiologist Assistants was formed. That's the N C C A A. It runs the certifying exam, which is administered through the National Board of Medical Examiners, the same organization behind the medical boards. Today every program is a master's program, affiliated with a medical school and accredited through CAAHEP. Students finish with at least two thousand clinical hours and around six hundred cases before graduation.

After you're certified, you maintain it with forty hours of continuing medical education every two years, and a recertification exam at regular intervals. In other words, the learning doesn't stop at graduation, and you should say you're glad about that.
Now, the heart of it. The anesthesia care team model. The A C T model. You need to be able to explain this simply, because there's a decent chance someone asks you to.

In the care team model, a physician anesthesiologist leads. Under that physician, you have non-physician anesthetists. That's C A As and C R N As, nurse anesthetists, plus residents at teaching hospitals. The anesthesiologist medically directs several rooms at once. Historically, the model was built around one anesthesiologist directing up to four rooms. The actual ratio depends on the state and on billing rules. Medicare, for example, requires the anesthesiologist to be immediately available.

In practice, it looks like what you saw. The anesthesiologist and the C A A meet the patient and agree on a plan. The anesthesiologist is present for the critical moments, like induction. Then the C A A stays in the room for the whole case, managing the anesthetic minute to minute, while the anesthesiologist moves between rooms, checks in, covers breaks, and comes back for anything that needs them. You saw an attending covering two rooms in July, and three rooms on August thirty-first. You saw Karissa handle emergence on her own while her attending was in another room. That's the model.

What does a C A A actually do? Pre-anesthetic evaluation, taking a history and doing an exam. Inducing and maintaining anesthesia. Airway management, including intubation. Placing lines and setting up advanced monitoring. Regional anesthesia under the anesthesiologist's direction. Emergence, handoff to recovery, and post-op checks. Basically the full arc of a case, every day.
Now, the comparison you'll definitely think about, and might get asked about. C A As versus C R N As.

Here's the clean version. Within the care team, the American Society of Anesthesiologists says C A As and C R N As have the same scope. They do the same work, they cover the same cases, and they relieve each other for breaks. There's a well-known study from twenty eighteen, published in the journal Anesthesiology, by Sun and colleagues. It compared care teams that used C A As with care teams that used C R N As. They found no significant differences in mortality, length of stay, or spending. Same outcomes.

The difference is the path, and the practice setting. C R N As come up through nursing. They work as I C U nurses, then do a doctoral nurse anesthesia program. C A As come through a pre-medical undergrad, then a master's program, and their training is designed by anesthesiologists, for the physician-led team. And C A As always practice within that team, under an anesthesiologist. In some states, C R N As can also practice on their own.

There's real politics here. The nurse anesthetist professional organization has historically opposed C A A licensure when it comes up in new states. You might get asked about it. The right tone is respectful and boring. Never trash C R N As. You'll work next to them for your whole career. Something like: "From what I've seen, the best rooms are the ones where everyone's excellent at their job and knows their role. I want to be part of a team, and that's what the C A A role is built for."

Where's the profession now? According to the American Academy of Anesthesiologist Assistants, as of this fall, C A As can practice in twenty-two states, plus Washington D C and Guam. It keeps growing. Nevada authorized C A As in twenty twenty-three. Virginia and Tennessee both came in twenty twenty-five. Washington State adopted practice rules that same year. New programs keep opening too, like Lipscomb in Nashville and Kansas City University in Joplin.

And Georgia is one of the profession's strongholds. It's a licensure state, it has two programs, Emory and South University in Savannah, and Atlanta has a big C A A workforce. That's not true where you're from. In Utah there are three practicing C A As, and you shadowed two of them. That contrast is a nice detail to keep in your back pocket.

A couple of career realities, so you sound informed. The pay is strong. The C A A you shadowed in July said the University of Utah pays on the lower end, in the two thirty to two fifty range, and other markets pay more. You don't need to bring up money in an interview, and you shouldn't lead with it. But it's good to know. Lifestyle varies. Some people work regular hospital schedules with call. Some, like Karissa, do travel or locums work, moving around the country eight to ten times a year. The profession is flexible.

One more thing. The weird part of the job. You saw it. Hours of steady vigilance, then a few minutes where everything matters. Interviewers love it when you show you understand that rhythm. Your cautery story is perfect for this. The monitor showed artifact, and Karissa wasn't treating the monitor, she was interpreting it.

Okay, let's lock it in. Three things you should be able to say in one breath. One: the profession started in nineteen sixty-nine at Emory and Case Western, to solve a provider shortage with a team. Two: the care team is physician-led, and C A As and C R N As do the same work inside it, with the same outcomes. Three: the profession is growing state by state, and Georgia is one of its homes.

Now, one practice question. This is one of the best ones you could get, because you've already watched someone answer it for real. Picture the husband from August thirty-first. Your proctor is going to play a family member.
I'm sorry, I'm a little confused. You're not the doctor? So who's actually doing my wife's anesthesia today?

Here's what Karissa did, and it's what you want to do. Answer directly, no defensiveness, in plain words. "I'm a certified anesthesiologist assistant. I'll be with your wife the whole time she's asleep. Dr. so-and-so is the anesthesiologist leading her care. He's overseeing a few rooms today, he'll be here for the important parts, and one of us is with her at every moment." Then check that they understood. If an interviewer asks you to explain the care team model, this exact answer works. Just say it to them instead.
That's day two. Tomorrow is the big one: why C A A. See you then.

title: Day 3 · Why anesthesia, why CAA
lines: Day three. Today's question is going to come up at Emory. I'd bet on it. Why anesthesia, and why a C A A specifically?

Here's what interviewers are actually listening for. First, that the reason is specific, and comes from something you saw or did, not a general idea about helping people. Second, that you understand the role, including the care team. Third, that this is a choice and not a fallback. Fourth, that you know what the hard parts are and want the job anyway.
Your answer has three layers. Let's build them one at a time.

Layer one. Why anesthesia. Your strongest material is the ephedrine moment from your shadowing. Quick refresher. A patient's blood pressure dropped at the start of a colostomy repair. Systolic in the seventies. The alarm went off. The C A A had ephedrine drawn up, and she didn't give it. She leaned over and told you to watch what happens when the surgeon makes the first cut. The surgeon called the incision, and the pressure came right back up to one ten over seventy. She'd expected the surgical stimulus to trigger a sympathetic response.

Why that moment matters is the real answer. It's physiology happening live, and someone who understood it well enough to trust it over an alarm. You studied that physiology in exercise science. You saw the same kind of judgment in detox, where a rising COWS score didn't automatically mean another Subutex dose, because what mattered was where the patient was heading. That's what draws you to anesthesia. Real-time physiology, and the judgment to act on where the patient is going.

Layer two. Why the C A A role. Two pieces. One, the responsibility thread. Under anesthesia, a patient can't do anything for themselves. Every part of their safety is on the team. That's the most complete version of what you've been doing as a caregiver and an interpreter. Two, the care team itself. You like the idea of giving one patient your full attention, with a physician backing you up who's a second set of eyes whenever you need it. Use your words from the personal statement. Continuous, singular attention, backed by a second set of eyes.

Layer three. Why not something else. This is where people get nervous, but you're in a great spot here, because you can be honest. You were on a P A track for years, and they'll see that on your resume. Own it. Don't hide it.

Here's the shape. "I spent years building toward P A, and I'm glad I did, because that's how I got all my patient care experience. But P A is broad, and when I started shadowing in anesthesia, I realized the part of medicine I love most is the physiology and pharmacology happening in the moment. P A would have kept me near that. C A A puts me right in it."

For C R N A, the honest answer is about the path. That route goes through a nursing degree and years of I C U work. You came up the pre-med path, and C A A is the role designed for exactly that background, built by anesthesiologists for the physician-led team. That team is the model you actually want to work in.

And for medicine, if they ask why not be the anesthesiologist. Keep it simple and positive. You want to be the one in the room, managing the anesthetic minute to minute, and you want to get there in two years, not twelve. And you genuinely like being on a team where someone with more training has your back. Never make it sound like medical school was too hard. Make it sound like this role fits you better.

Check yourself. Did you tell the ephedrine story, or at least a piece of it? Did you name the physiology, the sympathetic response to incision? And did you connect it to yourself? The story is only half the answer. The other half is why it grabbed you specifically.
Okay. But why an anesthesiologist assistant, specifically?

The two pieces were the responsibility thread and the care team. If you only talked about anesthesia, you answered the last question twice. The C A A part is the team. Full attention on one patient, with a physician backing you up. Bonus points if you used a real moment, like the attending stepping into the room mid-case to ask whether the C A A needed anything.
I noticed a lot of your experience is aimed at P A school. Is this your backup plan?

This is the one to nail, because it's a little bit of a challenge. The tone you want is relaxed and honest, not defensive. Something like: "No. Honestly, it's the other way around. P A was the plan before I knew this job existed. Once I shadowed, it wasn't close." Then give one specific reason. The physiology in real time, or the team. And here's a real point in your favor. You're applying only to C A A programs now. You can say so plainly. "This is the only thing I'm applying to." That's a strong signal.
What do you think will be the hardest part of this job for you?

Good answers pick something real and show you've thought about it. A few options for you. The rhythm: long stretches of vigilance, and then moments where everything happens at once. Staying sharp through the quiet part is a skill. Or being responsible for a patient who can't tell you anything is wrong, so all your information comes from monitors and physiology, and the monitors can lie, like the cautery artifact you saw. Or the pace of the program itself. Pick one, say why, and say what you'd do about it. Don't say you can't think of anything hard.
Last one. As a C A A, you'll always practice under an anesthesiologist. How do you feel about never working independently?

This is a gift of a question, because you've seen the answer. On August thirty-first, Karissa planned a supraglottic airway. Her attending recommended video laryngoscopy instead. She disagreed a little on the merits, and she switched anyway, without arguing, because extra caution cost nothing. And later, at emergence, she was already treating the patient before the surgeon even said anything, with her attending in another room. So the autonomy is real, moment to moment. And the backup is real too. You can say: "That's the version of autonomy I actually want." That's a great line. Use it.

Day three, done. If you only remember one thing: specific story, the care team, and a choice, not a fallback. Tomorrow is all about Emory itself, so you'll know exactly where you're walking into. See you then.

title: Day 4 · Emory, the program
lines: Day four. Today is all Emory. What the program is, how it's built, what the numbers say, what your interview day will look like, and what you should ask them. Two practice questions at the end.

Let's start with the basics. The degree is a Master of Medical Science in Anesthesiology. Emory calls it a concentrated graduate medical education program, run inside the Emory University School of Medicine, in the Department of Anesthesiology. You'd start in August twenty twenty-seven and finish in December twenty twenty-nine. That's seven semesters, twenty-seven continuous months. Continuous is the key word. There's no summer off.

The program isn't on Emory's main campus. It's at fifty-seven Executive Park South, Suite three hundred, off Interstate eighty-five, a few miles from main campus. The invitation even says, in bold, don't go to the main campus on Clifton Road. Remember that the morning of.

Now, how the twenty-seven months are built. The first four semesters mix coursework, hands-on skills labs, and human patient simulation, with semester-long clinical rotations in metro Atlanta running alongside. By the end of semester four, students have at least five hundred clinical hours. So you're in the O R early, while you're still learning the science.

That's worth noticing, because it's different from some programs. From your shadowing in July, you learned that N S U holds off on pairing classroom work with O R time until the second year. Emory puts you in the O R while you're in class. If that appeals to you, and it should, because you learn by applying things, that's a real reason to want Emory. Just don't knock another program to say it. Say what you like about Emory's approach, not what you dislike about anyone else's.

Semesters five through seven, the final twelve months, are full-time clinical rotations, with monthly peer-led seminars. Those rotations happen in metro Atlanta and at out-of-town sites. There are required rotations in cardiac, obstetric, and pediatric anesthesia, along with general surgery and a variety of other options. The clinical sites include Emory-owned hospitals, major affiliates, academic medical centers, and private practice settings.

Cardiac is a fun connection for you. Your first exposure to the head of the bed was a heart transplant. Cardiac anesthesia is required at Emory, and Emory Healthcare is a big cardiac center. If someone asks what part of anesthesia you're most curious about, cardiac is an honest, natural answer.

Now, the numbers. Emory's outcomes for twenty twenty-three through twenty twenty-five: a ninety-eight percent first-time pass rate on the national certifying exam, a hundred percent overall pass rate, a hundred percent job placement, and ninety-five percent retention. In plain words, they get people through, they get them certified, and they get them hired.

Admissions numbers, so you know where you stand. Last cycle, Emory got about twenty-four hundred applications. Around seven hundred were complete and verified. They interviewed about a hundred and sixty people, and made forty offers, for a class of up to forty-two. So getting an interview already puts you in roughly the top quarter of complete applicants. Of the people they interview, roughly one in four gets an offer. It's competitive, but the interview is now the whole game.

Their current first-year class, the class of twenty twenty-eight, has thirty-nine students. The average G P A is three point seven five overall, and three point seven science. Your three point nine four is above both. Their average G R E quant is one fifty-nine point two. Your new quant score is one sixty-one. That's above their average, so if anyone brings up your G R E, you're in a strong spot. The average age at matriculation is twenty-four. And about three quarters of the class is from the Southeast. You'd be one of the few westerners in the room. That's not a problem. It just means your answer to "why Emory, why Atlanta" needs to be real.

The program's academic program director is Dr. Katie Monroe, a C A A herself, with a P h D. She did a podcast interview this February about Emory's program. You don't need to name-drop her. But if she's in the room, it's good to recognize the name.

Now, your interview day. You check in at eleven forty-five Eastern. That's nine forty-five Utah time, so your body clock is on your side. Up to three hours. Business attire. Eight candidates per session. The day includes a program information session, formal interview breakouts, a group Q and A, Q and A with current students, a tour of the learning space, and light refreshments.

Here's the thing about a day like that. You're being watched the whole three hours, not just in the breakout. The student Q and A is not a break. Students often give feedback. Be the person who's curious, who asks good questions, who's warm with the other seven candidates. Don't compete with them out loud. In a care team program, how you treat your peers is part of the evaluation.
Let's talk about your questions for them. You'll have at least two chances to ask, in the group Q and A and with students. Have five ready. Here are good ones for you.

For faculty. One. How are the out-of-town rotations in the final year assigned, and how much input do students have? Two. Since clinical rotations start alongside classes in the first four semesters, what do the students who thrive in that first year do differently? Three. How is the simulation center used across the program? Is it mostly early, or does it continue into the clinical year? Four. Where do most of your graduates end up working, and how many stay in Georgia?

For current students. One. What does a normal week look like in your first semester? Two. Where do most students live, and how bad is the commute to clinical sites? Three. What surprised you most about the program? Four. What do you wish you'd done the summer before starting? That last one is a great question, because it shows you're already thinking like a student there.
And one question to avoid. Anything you could have answered by reading their website. Don't ask how long the program is.
Now, let's build your "why Emory" answer. Three parts. Something about the program, something about the place, and something about you that fits.
The program: it's one of the two places the profession started, it has excellent outcomes, and it puts you in the O R early, alongside the classroom, which is how you learn best.

The place: Atlanta is a huge, diverse clinical environment. Georgia is a licensure state with a deep C A A workforce. And there's a large Spanish-speaking community in metro Atlanta. Buford Highway, the corridor known for its Latino and immigrant communities, runs just a few miles from Executive Park. Your Spanish is a patient safety tool in a pre-op interview, and Atlanta is a place where you'd actually use it.

You: you and your wife want this move. You're both excited about an East Coast adventure, and the South fits you better than cold places. Keep this light. One sentence. And a warning from your earlier writing work: don't frame Atlanta as a stepping stone back to Utah. Frame it as where you want to train.
We interview a lot of strong people. Why Emory?

Check. Did you say something only true about Emory? "Great outcomes" is true of lots of programs. "One of the two original programs" and "clinical rotations from the first semester" are specific. Did you connect Atlanta's Spanish-speaking community to something you've actually done? And did you sound like you want to live there, not just study there?
We're about out of time. What questions do you have for me?

Never say "I think you've covered everything." Ask one or two real questions, then thank them. A small trick: if something came up earlier in the interview, ask about that. It shows you were listening.
That's Emory. Tomorrow we start your experience bank, with your first three stories. See you then.

title: Day 5 · Experience bank, part 1
lines: Day five. Today we start your experience bank. You built six stories for CASPer, and they're good. The job now is making them interview-shaped, because an interview is different from CASPer in one big way. In an interview, every story needs to land on why it makes you a good future C A A.

Here's the structure for every story. Four parts. Situation, in one or two sentences. Don't over-set the scene. What you did, which gets most of your time, and should be specific actions, in order. What happened as a result. And then the bridge, one sentence connecting it to anesthesia or to the program. The bridge is the part most applicants skip, and it's the part that makes interviewers write things down.
Target about ninety seconds per story. If you're over two minutes, you're telling them what the room looked like.
Today: three stories. The no-show phone call, the baptism disagreement, and the software crisis.
Story one. The no-show phone call. This is your empathy story.

Quick recap. As a scribe, you called a patient who'd skipped his appointment. The second he picked up, you could tell from his tone that he wasn't okay. Instead of accepting the surface excuse, you drew out what was really going on. Then you reflected his own feelings back to him. The same feelings making him want to skip were exactly why the appointment mattered. And you left the choice with him.

What's great about it. You noticed something small, his tone. You didn't take the easy answer. And you didn't pressure him. That last part matters a lot. Leaving the choice with him is patient autonomy, which is the core of informed consent.

What to tighten. Say one concrete thing you actually said to him. Even a paraphrase. Something like, "I told him that the way he was feeling right then was exactly why it was worth showing up." Interviewers remember quotes. And have a result. Did he reschedule? Did he come in? If you don't know, say what you learned instead.

The bridge. A pre-op interview is a short conversation with a scared person, where you have to pick up on what they're not saying. Anxiety, a history they forgot to mention, a language barrier. Reading someone fast and accurately is a pre-op skill.
Story two. The baptism disagreement. This is your conflict and cross-cultural story, and it's one of your best.

Recap. Your mission companion rescheduled and extended invitations without consulting you, against what you'd agreed on. You didn't correct him in front of anyone. You waited until you were alone, and you led with curiosity. You asked about his thinking instead of accusing him. He connected his view to growing up in the church in Peru, which was a completely different experience from yours. Understanding that didn't change your position, but it changed how you worked together from then on.
Why it's strong. Private, not public. Curiosity before judgment. And you didn't cave. You held your position and still built a better relationship. That's mature.

Here's the upgrade that will make it great for anesthesia. Add one line about when you would not wait for privacy. In an O R, a safety concern gets raised right then, in the moment, out loud. A difference in working style waits for a private conversation. Something like: "If it had been a safety issue, I would have said something right there. Since it was about how we worked together, I waited until we could talk alone." That one line shows you understand how an operating room works. It also lines up with what a C A A told you in July: escalate early, even if it feels annoying.

The bridge. In the care team you'll work with anesthesiologists, surgeons, nurses, and C R N As, from every kind of background. Sometimes you'll disagree. You know how to handle that without damaging the team.
Story three. The software crisis. This is your adaptability and initiative story.

Recap. One morning, a forced update locked your whole team out of your documentation tool, with sixty patient notes due. You noticed the browser version still worked. You had coworkers handle prep so the day kept moving. You rebuilt the templates for the online tool and migrated every note. It's been the standard setup ever since.
Why it's strong. It has everything. Pressure, a real deadline, a creative fix, delegation, and a lasting result. Facility-wide adoption is concrete proof.

What to tighten. Order matters here. First you kept the clinic running, then you fixed the system. Say it in that order, because that's the right priority. Patients first, infrastructure second. And keep the technical details light. They don't need to know the software's name.

The bridge. Equipment fails in the O R. A pump alarms, a monitor drops out, a machine won't cooperate. The skill is the same. Keep the patient safe and the case moving first, and fix the system second. Delegating parts of it is part of that skill.
Now let's practice. The proctor won't tell you which story to use. Your job is to pick the right one fast. For these three, the match is pretty clear.
Tell me about a time you connected with a patient who was struggling.

That's story one, the phone call. Check: did you include the moment you noticed his tone? Did you quote yourself, even roughly? Did you leave the choice with him, and say that out loud? And did you bridge to the pre-op conversation?
Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone you worked closely with. How did you handle it?

Story two. Check: did you add the safety line, the part about when you would speak up right away? That's the upgrade. Did you say what you learned about his background, without making him sound wrong? And did you say you held your position? That matters. They don't want someone who caves.
Tell me about a time something went wrong and you had to adapt quickly.
Story three. Check: did you keep the clinic running first, then fix the system? Did you say you delegated? And did you end on the result, that it became the standard? That's your proof.
Now a twist. Same stories, different questions. This is the real skill. Interviewers ask in a hundred ways, and your stories stretch. Just pick the closest one.
Tell me about a time you worked with someone from a very different background than yours.

Best fit is story two, the companion from Peru. This time, put the cross-cultural part in the spotlight. Less about the conflict, more about what you learned from understanding where he came from. You could also use interpreting, which is cross-cultural every single shift.
Describe a time you showed leadership without having a formal title.
Story three works well. Nobody made you the lead that morning. You saw the fix and organized people around it. That's leadership without a title. Point that out.
Day five, done. You've got three stories in shape. Tomorrow: the other three, plus a speed drill where you match stories to questions on the fly.

title: Day 6 · Experience bank, part 2 + speed matching
lines: Day six. The other half of your experience bank. The avoided patient, the five-day housing scramble, and the two hundred dollar deficit. Then a speed drill.
Same structure as yesterday. Situation, short. What you did, most of the time. The result. Then the bridge to anesthesia.
Story four. The avoided patient. This is your integrity and escalation story.

Recap. A provider was avoiding a frequent-complaint patient by sending everything through the nurses. It wasn't your place to correct a doctor. So instead of staying quiet or gossiping, you raised your concern through the proper channel, your supervisor.

Honest assessment. This is your weakest story, and that's fine. Every bank has one. Here's how to handle it. Use it only when they ask specifically about integrity, ethics, or speaking up. Keep it short, about a minute. And frame it entirely around your judgment, not around the doctor's failure. The story is about how you decided what to do, not about a bad doctor.

The framing sounds like this. "I noticed something that made me uncomfortable about how a patient was getting care. I had three options. Say nothing, talk about it with coworkers, or bring it to the right person. It wasn't my role to correct a physician, so I brought it to my supervisor, and let them handle it from there."

Don't describe the doctor's personality. Don't say the patient was annoying. And if you know what happened afterward, say it briefly. If you don't, that's okay. What you learned is that escalating through the right channel protects the patient and keeps the team intact.
The bridge is strong, actually. In the care team, escalation has a clear path. Concerns go to the anesthesiologist. You already respect that structure.
Story five. The five-day housing scramble. This is your teamwork-under-pressure story, and it's an A.

Recap. As mission housing coordinator, you'd get five days' notice to house four missionaries in an area with no home, often without knowing exactly how many were coming or when. You got the fixed requirements from the mission president. You mobilized nearby missionaries and local leaders to search. You coordinated furniture and transport. You kept the president updated at every step. And when the timing slipped, you built backup housing using travel funds.
The key line, and you already have it, is this: you acted on what was certain instead of freezing over what wasn't. Say that sentence, almost word for word. It's excellent.

What to tighten. Pick one specific time. Even if you did this many times, telling one specific scramble makes it real. And it was in Ecuador, in Spanish, with local leaders. Mention that, because it shows you can lead across language and culture.

The bridge. In anesthesia you're constantly deciding with incomplete information. The surgeon might take an hour or three. Blood loss might be fifty milliliters or a liter. You plan for what you know, prepare for what you don't, and keep the team informed. That's this story.
Story six. The two hundred dollar deficit. This is your failure story. Every interview has a failure question, and this is a good answer, because it's a real mistake with a real fix.

Recap. While running mission finances in a chaotic period, you covered some expenses with your own money, planning to pay yourself back. You lost track on paper and ended up two hundred dollars short, no matter how you ran the numbers. You told the mission president the moment he was free. Together you figured out what caused it. And you set two rules. A system rule: never use personal funds again. And a personal rule: delegate before you hit overload.
Why it works. You own it right away. You report it fast. You fix the system, not just the moment. And you learned something about yourself. That's exactly what interviewers want in a failure story.

Two cautions. One, keep the money details simple and leave the tithing piece out, like you planned. Two, don't make it sound too small. The point isn't the two hundred dollars. The point is that something you were responsible for didn't add up, and you reported it immediately instead of hiding it.

The bridge is powerful for anesthesia, so use it. "In anesthesia, that same rule applies to medication errors and controlled substance counts. If something doesn't add up, you report it the minute you know. I learned that with two hundred dollars, which is a cheap way to learn it."
And bonus. This story also answers the weakness question. Your weakness is taking on too much before you delegate. Story six is the proof that you know it and you've built a fix.

Now, the speed drill. The proctor will fire off questions. For each one, you get a short pause. Don't tell the whole story. Just say out loud which story you'd use and the first sentence of it. Then I'll say what I'd pick.
Tell me about a time you failed.
Tell me about a time you led a team.
Story five, housing. Story three works too.
Tell me about a time you had to make a decision without all the information.
Story five. That's the whole point of it.
Tell me about an ethical dilemma you faced.
Story four, the avoided patient. Keep it short.
Tell me about a time you received difficult feedback.
Story six. The feedback came from diagnosing the problem with your president. Story two works too, if you frame his perspective as feedback on your assumptions.
Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a patient.
Story one, the phone call. Or interpreting, if you have a specific moment.
Tell me about the most stressful situation you've been in.
Story three, or story five. Both have a ticking clock.
Tell me about a time you had to speak up.
Story four. Or story two, with the safety line.
Now one full story, start to finish. This is the one you'll almost certainly get.
Tell me about a mistake you made, and what you learned from it.

Check. Did you report it fast, in the story? Did you name both rules, the system one and the personal one? And did you land the anesthesia bridge, about medication errors and counts? If yes, that's an interview-winning answer.
Day six, done. Your whole bank is built. Six stories, and each one covers several questions. Tomorrow is about owning your application, starting with your shadowing.

title: Day 7 · Owning your application: shadowing
lines: Day seven. Today and tomorrow are about owning your application. Interviewers will have read it, and some will pick a line and ask you about it. Today is your shadowing, which is the most likely thing they'll dig into, because it's the best evidence you understand the job.

Let's walk through what you've seen, so it's fresh. You have three experiences. The heart transplant, years ago. About twenty hours with C A As at the University of Utah in July. And about ten hours on August thirty-first with Karissa. Know those numbers roughly, in case someone asks how much you've shadowed. Around thirty hours with C A As, plus the transplant.
July, at the University of Utah. A dental O R. Two cases worth remembering.

The first patient was a forty-year-old man with cerebral palsy, who couldn't cooperate with a normal induction. They started with an I M ketamine injection to calm him, and the first dose barely touched him. The team split up. The C A A got consent from his parents while the anesthesiologist talked the patient through the shot. Because it was dental surgery, they intubated through the nose, to keep the tube out of the surgical field, using a video laryngoscope and Magill forceps. His large tongue made it harder. Then, near the end, the anesthesiologist couldn't be there for wake-up. So about fifteen minutes before emergence, they briefed the surgeon, and the C A A and the circulating nurse handled the whole wake-up and handoff themselves.

The second patient was a twenty-eight-year-old man, autistic and needle-phobic. His case had been cancelled once before because he became combative. This time he asked for a blood draw while he was asleep, so he wouldn't have to face a needle awake. That's a great small detail. Anesthesia isn't just for surgery. It's how you make care possible for someone who couldn't otherwise get it. That fits your thread perfectly. People who can't fully care for themselves.

That intubation was hard too. It took three people. The anesthesiologist held the scope, the C A A guided the tube with forceps, and a third provider pushed rocuronium to relax the cords. When the blood pressure dropped, she gave phenylephrine without missing a beat. And she gave antibiotics before the surgeon asked, because she saw that the extractions were coming next.

And the ephedrine case. From your personal statement. The colostomy repair, pressure in the seventies, the alarm going off, and the C A A holding the ephedrine because she knew the incision would bring the pressure up. That's your signature moment. You've practiced it already.
August thirty-first, with Karissa. Breast surgical oncology. Three cases under general anesthesia. Her attending was covering three rooms.

The moments to remember. The patient's husband asking, "so who's the anesthesiologist," and Karissa explaining the care team at the bedside. Karissa planning a supraglottic airway, her attending suggesting video laryngoscopy, and Karissa switching without argument. The electrocautery putting artifact on the E E G and heart rate monitors, and Karissa interpreting the numbers instead of treating them. And at emergence, the surgeon calling out that the patient was coughing, and Karissa already pushing propofol.
Now, three cautions. These matter, because a knowledgeable interviewer will catch them.

Caution one. In your notes from August, the first patient's propranolol was held for five days before surgery. Don't repeat that detail. Current guidance is to continue beta blockers through surgery, because stopping them suddenly can cause rebound fast heart rate and high blood pressure. Something got lost in translation that day. If you mention her history at all, keep it general. Hypertension and diabetes.
Caution two. Those cases were listed as possible axillary node dissections. From what you saw, they stopped at sentinel node biopsy. Describe them that way. Lumpectomies with sentinel node biopsy.

Caution three. This one is actually an opportunity. Your personal statement ends a paragraph with, "It may be the surgeon's operation, but it is the anesthesia team's patient." Someone may ask about that line. And here's the thing. On August thirty-first, Karissa's attending pushed back on exactly that idea. He called the relationship symbiotic. The surgeons bring the patients, and they know them long before anesthesia does. In the moment of the case, though, the framing is partly right.

So if they ask about that line, you get to show maturity. Something like: "I wrote that after my first shadowing. Then an attending pushed back on it, and I think he's right that it's more of a partnership. The surgeon has known that patient for weeks. But during the case, the anesthesia team is responsible for keeping them alive, so I still think the line holds in that moment." That answer shows you take feedback and think in nuance. Interviewers love that.
Tell me about your shadowing experience.

Check. Did you give a rough sense of hours and settings? Did you tell one specific moment, rather than listing everything? And did you say what you learned about the role, not just what you watched? The best answers here end on an insight. For example: explaining the care team model is part of practicing in it.
What surprised you most when you shadowed?

Good honest options. How quiet and steady most of the case is, and then how fast it moves at induction and emergence. Or that the family didn't know what a C A A was, so patient education is part of the job. Or how much the C A A ran the room independently, with the anesthesiologist checking in. Pick one. Make it something real.
In your personal statement, you wrote that it may be the surgeon's operation, but it's the anesthesia team's patient. Can you tell me more about what you meant?

Did you use the attending's pushback? That's the move. You stand by the line in the moment of the case, and you add the nuance that it's really a partnership. That's a much better answer than just defending the line.
Walk me through what the C A A did during one case you observed, from start to finish.

This tests whether you were paying attention. A good walk-through: the pre-op conversation and consent, the plan agreed with the attending, induction and the airway, maintenance, which was propofol and remifentanil in many of your cases, watching the field and anticipating things like antibiotics, the attending checking in, then emergence and handoff. You don't need drug doses. You need the flow. If you got the order right, you understand the job.
Day seven, done. Tomorrow is the rest of your application: your work, your activities, and the soft spots, so nothing surprises you.

title: Day 8 · Owning your application: experience + soft spots
lines: Day eight. The rest of your application, plus the soft spots. By the end of today, nothing on your application should be able to surprise you.
First, a quick tour of what's there, so you remember what you can draw from. You'll notice you have more than you think.

Resilience Health. Scribe and medical assistant since June twenty twenty-five, at a behavioral health startup. You rotated through three settings. A behavioral hospital seeing seventy to eighty patients a day. A post-acute telehealth clinic. And an inpatient detox unit. You did intake and follow-up conversations, and you rebuilt the documentation system that's now used facility-wide. If someone asks about your clinical experience, this is the center of it. The detox unit is especially useful, because it's where you saw dosing decisions based on where a patient was heading. That's anesthesia thinking.

Midvale C B C Community Clinic. Volunteer Spanish medical interpreter since April twenty twenty-five, ten or more patients a shift. Diagnoses, treatment plans, medication instructions. This is your second-strongest asset after shadowing, because it connects directly to a safe pre-op interview for patients with limited English.

Home care. In twenty twenty-four, you were an in-home caregiver for a C five-six quadriplegic client. That's where you learned that the order of the steps is itself the safety mechanism. That's a great line for anesthesia, which is full of checklists and sequences.

And the rest. Your mission in Guayaquil, Ecuador. Leading a refugee care team. Teaching English classes. Directing in the B Y U Student Association. Literacy tutoring this fall, with a third-grade Latino boy, twice a week. Eagle Scout. Any of these can come up. You don't need stories for all of them. Just be ready to say in two sentences what you did and what you got out of it.

Now, the soft spots. Most won't come up. But if one does, the rule is the same every time. Short, honest, no excuses, then pivot to what you did about it. Twenty to thirty seconds. Never longer. Long answers make a small thing look big.

Soft spot one. Your G R E. You took it once in May without studying, and got a one fifty-seven in quant. Then you retook it in July and got one sixty-four verbal and one sixty-one quant. Their incoming class averaged one fifty-nine point two in quant. So you're above their average now. If it comes up: "The first time, I honestly didn't prepare. I retook it, prepared properly, and brought my quant up four points." Done. That's a story of taking something seriously, not a weakness.

Soft spot two. Outstanding prerequisites. You're taking biochemistry this fall, and calculus and physics two this winter. You graduate in April twenty twenty-seven, well before an August start. If asked: "I'm in biochem now, and I'll finish calculus and physics two this winter. I graduate in April." Say it plainly. If you're doing well in biochem, say so. It's the class most related to pharmacology.

Soft spot three. A couple of prerequisites are technical edge cases. Your biology one course didn't include a lab, and your physics one came from A P credit, so it shows as a pass. These are paperwork questions, and it's unlikely they come up in a breakout. If they do: "I know those are a bit unusual. I'm happy to take whatever you'd want me to before starting." That's the whole answer. Showing flexibility is the point.

Soft spot four. No research. Lots of applicants don't have research. If it comes up, don't apologize. Say your experience has been clinical and patient-facing, and then show you read the literature. For your N S U application, you summarized a twenty twenty-six Anesthesia and Analgesia study on gastric ultrasound in patients taking G L P one drugs like Ozempic before anesthesia. That's a perfect thing to mention. G L P one drugs slow stomach emptying, which raises aspiration risk, and it's a hot topic in anesthesia right now. Three points you remember from that paper. The ultrasound only modestly predicted a full stomach. There were no actual aspiration events, so they measured a substitute outcome. And they screened over fourteen thousand patients down to about three hundred, so selection bias is a real question. Being able to critique a study like that tells them you can read research, even if you haven't done it.

Soft spot five. You found this profession recently. Some interviewers will notice that most of your experience was built for P A. Your answer is that you found it late, but you checked it out carefully. You shadowed in two different settings, your brother-in-law is an anesthesiologist, and you read up on the field. Late, but deliberate.
What would you say is your biggest weakness?

The weakness that fits you, and that's true, is taking on too much yourself before you delegate. Story six is the proof, and so are the two rules you made. Name the weakness, give the example quickly, and say what you do differently now. Don't use a fake weakness like "I work too hard." They've heard it a thousand times.
I see your quant score is lower than your verbal. Talk to me about that.
Short and confident. You retook it, prepared, and improved four points, and you're now above their class average. Then stop talking. Don't over-explain math anxiety or anything like that.
You still have a few prerequisites left. How are you planning to handle that alongside everything else?

Plain facts. Biochem this fall, calculus and physics two this winter, graduating in April. Then something that shows you can handle the load. You've kept a three point nine four while working clinically the whole time. That's the evidence that you can handle a heavy schedule.
You don't have any research experience. Why not?
Did you mention the G L P one paper? That's your move. Don't apologize. Say your experience was clinical, then show you can think critically about research.
Is there anything in your application you'd want us to notice that we might have missed?

This is a free shot, so take it. Pick the thing that matters most to you and that's easy to skim past. For you, it's probably the interpreting. Five years of Spanish, used in clinic, directly relevant to pre-op safety. Or the documentation rebuild at work, which shows initiative. One thing, said with conviction.
Day eight, done. You now own your whole application, including the parts you'd rather not talk about. Tomorrow is a relaxing listening day all about Atlanta. See you then.

title: Day 9 · Atlanta and Emory, the story
lines: Day nine. Easy one today. Just listen. This is the story of Atlanta, Emory, and the neighborhood you'd be training in. Not for memorizing. It's so that when someone asks what you know about Atlanta, or you're making small talk on the tour, you sound like someone who's actually thought about living there.

Let's start with how Atlanta got its start, because it's kind of a funny origin. Atlanta wasn't founded on a river or a harbor like most big American cities. It was founded because of a railroad. In eighteen thirty-seven, surveyors drove a stake into the ground to mark the end point of a new railroad line, the Western and Atlantic. The little settlement that grew up around it was literally called Terminus. A few years later it was renamed Marthasville, after a governor's daughter. And then, in the mid eighteen forties, it got the name Atlanta, a feminine form of Atlantic, from that same railroad.

That railroad origin explains a lot about the city to this day. Atlanta has always been a crossroads. Railroads first, then highways, and now the airport. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International is one of the busiest airports in the world, usually number one by passenger count. Practically, for you, that means flying home to Utah or anywhere else is easy, with direct flights everywhere.

The crossroads idea is also why Atlanta mattered so much in the Civil War. It was a supply and rail hub for the Confederacy. In eighteen sixty-four, General William Tecumseh Sherman captured the city, and much of it burned before he began his March to the Sea toward Savannah. Fun connection: Savannah, where you interview second, is where that march ended. After the war, Atlanta rebuilt fast. The city's symbol is a phoenix rising from ashes, and its motto is Resurgens, Latin for "rising again." Atlanta became Georgia's state capital in eighteen sixty-eight.

Here's a story that ties directly to Emory. In eighteen eighty-six, an Atlanta pharmacist named John Pemberton created a syrup he sold at a soda fountain downtown. That was Coca-Cola. The company was later bought by a businessman named Asa Candler, who built it into a giant. And Asa Candler's brother, Warren Candler, was a Methodist bishop and a former president of a small college called Emory.

Emory College started in eighteen thirty-six, in a small town called Oxford, Georgia, about forty miles east of Atlanta. It was founded by Methodists. Then, in nineteen fifteen, Asa Candler gave a million dollars and a big piece of land in the Druid Hills area of Atlanta. Emory moved there and became Emory University. Coca-Cola money, and later the Woodruff family, also connected to Coca-Cola, shaped Emory into one of the best-funded research universities in the country. Oxford College still exists, by the way, as a small campus of Emory.

Emory today is a major research university, and Emory Healthcare is one of the largest health systems in Georgia. Two neighbors are worth knowing. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the C D C, has its headquarters right next to Emory's main campus on Clifton Road. Emory donated land for it back in the nineteen forties. So the national center for public health sits next door. And Grady Memorial Hospital, downtown, is one of the largest public hospitals in the country, a big Level One trauma center, staffed by Emory and Morehouse School of Medicine physicians. Grady takes care of a huge share of Atlanta's uninsured and underserved patients.

That's worth a moment, given what you care about. You've said you want to work with the patients who usually get the least. Atlanta has big, well-funded academic hospitals and also safety-net hospitals serving people with very little. You could see both in one training program. If it's natural, ask a student or faculty member what clinical sites like that look like for A A students.

Atlanta is also central to American civil rights history. Doctor Martin Luther King Junior was born in Atlanta in nineteen twenty-nine, on Auburn Avenue. He preached at Ebenezer Baptist Church, with his father. Morehouse College, where he studied, is in Atlanta. Today the King Center and his birth home are part of a national historical park. And Atlanta hosted the nineteen ninety-six Summer Olympics, which is why there's a Centennial Olympic Park downtown.
Now, the part that matters for daily life. Where you'd actually be.

The A A program is at Executive Park, northeast of downtown, off Interstate eighty-five, near North Druid Hills Road, close to Brookhaven. It's a few miles from the main Emory campus. Emory has been building Executive Park into a medical and academic hub.

Right nearby is Buford Highway. It's a long corridor running northeast through Brookhaven, Chamblee, and Doraville, famous for its immigrant communities and food. Mexican, Central American, Vietnamese, Korean, Chinese, and a lot more. For you, that means two things. Amazing cheap food. And a large Spanish-speaking community, close to where you'd train. Metro Atlanta has a large and growing Latino population, especially in the northeastern suburbs, like Gwinnett County.

Weather. You and your wife don't love the cold, and Atlanta is good news there. Summers are long, hot, and humid. Winters are mild, with occasional cold snaps, and snow is rare enough that one inch can shut down the city. Spring is beautiful, with flowering dogwoods everywhere. Atlanta is called a city in a forest, because it has one of the densest tree canopies of any major American city.

Getting around. Atlanta is a driving city, and the traffic is famous for being bad. The highways that ring the city, especially the I two eighty-five Perimeter, get backed up. Practical takeaway: when you'd pick housing, distance to clinical sites matters a lot. That's a perfect question for current students.

Cost of living. It's cheaper than big coastal cities like Boston or San Francisco, but it's been rising, and it's more expensive than Savannah. Rent in the neighborhoods near Executive Park varies a lot.

Weekends. You're two hours from the North Georgia mountains, the start of the Appalachian Trail at Springer Mountain, waterfalls, and lakes. You can be on the Gulf beaches or the Atlantic coast in a half-day drive. Savannah is about four hours away, and the Smoky Mountains are under four. For a couple who wants to adventure on the East Coast, Atlanta is a great base.

And for you and your wife personally. There's an Atlanta Georgia Temple in Sandy Springs, not far north of Executive Park. There's a strong network of wards across the metro area. So finding community would be easy.
That's Atlanta. One practice question, and it's an easy one.
You're coming from Utah. Have you thought about what it would be like to move all the way across the country for this?

The answer they want: yes, you've thought about it, your wife is on board and excited, and you have real reasons to want Atlanta, not just Emory. Pick one or two things from today that you actually liked. The weather, the adventure, the Spanish-speaking community. And skip anything about moving back to Utah later. Make it sound like you're coming to stay, at least for a while.
Day nine, done. Tomorrow is curveballs. Ethics questions, scenario questions, and the weird ones. See you then.

title: Day 10 · Curveballs, ethics, and scenarios
lines: Day ten. Curveballs. These are the questions you can't fully prepare for, so instead of answers, we'll practice a way of thinking that works for any of them.
Here's the framework for scenario and ethics questions. Five steps, and you say them out loud as you go, because the interviewer is grading your reasoning, not just your final answer.

One. Patient safety first. Ask yourself whether anyone is in danger right now. If yes, that comes before everything else. Two. Get the facts. Don't assume. There may be something you don't know. Three. Use the right channel. In the care team, concerns go to the anesthesiologist, then up the chain if needed. Four. Think about everyone involved, including the person you're worried about. Be fair to them. Five. Act, and follow up.

You don't need to name the steps. Just let them shape your answer. And one more tip. It's completely fine to pause for a few seconds before answering. A thoughtful pause looks good. Rushing into a scenario looks bad.
You're a C A A student. Before a case, you notice a classmate seems off, and you think you smell alcohol on their breath. What do you do?

Strong answer: patient safety comes first, so that classmate shouldn't be taking care of a patient right now. You'd talk to them privately, right away if you can. But if they're about to go into a case, you go straight to the supervising anesthesiologist or your clinical coordinator, because you don't have time to wait. You do it without accusing, sticking to what you observed. And you'd also care about your classmate. Impairment can mean someone's struggling, and programs have resources to help. Safety first, then compassion. Not one or the other.
Your supervising anesthesiologist asks you to do something during a case that you believe is unsafe. What do you do?

Speak up, right then, respectfully and clearly. Something like: "I'm concerned about this. Can we talk through it?" Most of the time, there's a reason you don't know about, and you'll learn something. That's step two, get the facts. If you still believe it's unsafe for the patient, you don't do it, and you escalate. But your tone is collaborative, not defiant. You can mention the airway story too. When the concern is just a difference in judgment, like Karissa's, you defer. When it's a real safety issue, you speak up. Knowing the difference is the skill.
During a case, you realize you gave a medication at the wrong time. Nobody noticed, and the patient seems fine. What do you do?

Tell your anesthesiologist immediately. Then monitor the patient for any effects, document it honestly, and report it through the hospital's system. Here's the line that makes this answer yours: it's story six. You learned with two hundred dollars that when something doesn't add up, you report it the minute you know. Reporting errors is how the whole system gets safer. Hiding them is how patients get hurt.
A Spanish-speaking patient is about to sign an anesthesia consent form. There's no interpreter. A nurse says the patient's teenage son can just translate. What do you think?

This one is your home turf, so if you get anything like it, be confident. Using a family member, especially a minor, isn't appropriate for consent. They might not know medical terms, they might filter bad news, and it puts the kid in an unfair position. The right move is a qualified interpreter, in person or by phone or video, which hospitals are required to provide. Then you can add what you've actually seen as an interpreter. Patients nod along when they don't understand. That's dangerous in a pre-op conversation. And if they ask whether you'd interpret yourself as a C A A, say your Spanish helps you connect and catch things, but for formal consent you'd follow the hospital's interpreter policy.

Be specific and real. What do you actually do? Exercise, which fits your degree. Time with your wife. Your faith. Music. And also how you handle stress in the moment, not just after. Under pressure, you break the problem down to what's certain and act on that, which is story five. That's a great answer, because it covers both. Recovering after, and functioning during.
This program is twenty-seven months straight, with almost no breaks, and you won't be able to work. How are you preparing for that?

Show them you know what you're getting into. You talked to C A As about it, and they told you that you can't work during the program, and there are basically no breaks. You and your wife have planned for it financially, and she's fully on board. You've kept a three point nine four while working clinically, so a heavy load isn't new to you. And say you're looking forward to it, not just bracing for it.
What will you do if you're not accepted this year?

Calm and committed. You'd ask for feedback, strengthen whatever was weakest, keep working clinically, get more shadowing, and reapply. The key message: this is what you want to do, and one cycle doesn't change that. Don't mention P A as a backup. You're only applying to C A A, so own that.
Last one. How do you think C A As and C R N As should work together?

Respectful and team-focused. Inside the care team, C A As and C R N As do the same work and relieve each other, and research shows the same outcomes. You'd want to learn from experienced C R N As, just like from anyone else. Don't wade into the politics. If they push, say you'd rather focus on being great at your job, and that the patient doesn't care which letters are on your badge. They care that you're paying attention.

Day ten, done. Here's the big idea. For any curveball, think out loud, put safety first, use the right channel, and be fair to everyone. If you do that, you can't really get one wrong. Tomorrow is the full mock interview. Wear something that's not pajamas, if you can. It helps.

title: Day 11 · Full mock interview
lines: Day eleven. Tomorrow's the day. Today is a full mock interview, start to finish. I'm going to step out of the way. The proctor runs the whole thing. No coaching between questions. Just like the real breakout.
Before we start, sit up, or stand if you're walking. Take one slow breath. Treat this like it's real. When it's over, I'll come back for a short debrief.
Hi Steven, thanks for coming in today. Thanks for traveling all the way from Utah. Let's just jump in. Tell me a little about yourself.
Great. So why do you want to be an anesthesiologist assistant?
Tell me about a time you made a mistake. What happened, and what did you learn?
Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone on your team.
Let's say I'm a patient's husband in the pre-op area, and I ask you who's actually doing my wife's anesthesia. Explain the care team to me.
What would your coworkers at Resilience Health say about you?
Is there anything else you'd like us to know about you?
Well, we're about at time. What questions do you have for me?
Thanks, Steven. It was great to meet you.
And that's the mock. How did it feel?
Quick debrief. Go through these in your head, and be honest.
One. Openers. Did "tell me about yourself" hit the four beats, under two minutes? Present, moment, thread, destination.

Two. Did you use at least two different stories from your bank, not the same one twice? Mistake should have been the two hundred dollars. Disagreement should have been your companion, with the safety line.
Three. Bridges. Did most of your answers end by connecting back to anesthesia or the care team?
Four. The husband question. Did you explain it in plain words, without defensiveness?

Five. Coworkers. That one wasn't in your prep, on purpose. A good answer is two or three traits with quick evidence. Probably reliable, the person who fixes things when they break, and calm with difficult patients. If you froze there, that's normal. That's what curveballs are for.
Six. Anything else we should know. Did you use it? It's a free shot. The interpreting, or how sure you are about this career, are both good.
Seven. Questions. Did you ask real ones? Did you thank them?

Now, open your tracker and mark how today felt. Then, if you have time, ask Ri to run three questions with you tonight. Just three. Your weakest from today, plus tell me about yourself and why Emory. Then stop. Don't cram. You're ready.

Some logistics for tomorrow, so your brain doesn't have to hold them. The address is fifty-seven Executive Park South, Suite three hundred. Not the main campus on Clifton Road. Check-in is eleven forty-five Eastern. Arrive no more than ten minutes early. Parking is free. Business attire. If you're checking out of your hotel first, you can bring your luggage with you. Get some sleep. Tomorrow morning there's one short track to warm up. See you then.

title: Day 12 · Interview morning warm-up
lines: Good morning, Steven. It's interview day. This one's short. Just a warm-up, so you walk in loose and ready.

First, logistics, one last time. Fifty-seven Executive Park South, Suite three hundred. Not Clifton Road. Check in at eleven forty-five, and don't arrive more than ten minutes early. That means eleven thirty-five at the earliest. Free parking. Bring your luggage in if you need to. And put your phone on silent before you walk in.
Now, let's wake up your voice. Your proctor will ask the opener. Answer it out loud, the way you'll say it in the room.
Good morning. So tell me about yourself.
Good. Present, moment, thread, destination. You've got it.
Here are three things to carry with you today. That's all. Three.

One. Be specific. Every time you're about to say something general, like "I love helping people," swap it for a moment. The ephedrine. The husband asking who the anesthesiologist was. The phone call. Specific beats impressive.
Two. Bridge it back. End your answers by connecting to the job. Safety, vigilance, the care team, the patient who can't speak for themselves.

Three. The whole three hours counts. The student Q and A, the tour, the refreshments. Be curious, be kind to the other candidates, and ask good questions. They're picking classmates, not just test-takers.

Now pick your anchor. One story you want them to hear today, no matter what they ask. For most people in your spot, it's the ephedrine moment, because it shows you understand the physiology and the role at the same time. Find a place for it.
Let's do one slow breathing round to settle your nerves. Breathe in for four counts. Hold for four. Out for four. Hold for four. I'll give you about twenty seconds.
Good. One more practice question, just to get the feel of a story.
Tell me about a time you had to make a decision without all the information.
That's the housing scramble. Act on what's certain instead of freezing over what isn't. Today, that's your motto too. You can't control which questions they ask. You can control how you show up.
One last thing for after. Try to remember the names of the faculty in your breakout. Tonight or tomorrow, send a short thank-you email to the program. Mention one specific thing from the day.
You've put in the work, Steven. You've got real stories, real experience, and real reasons to be there. Go show them. Good luck today.
